annotations.keyFindings: A nine-predictor model fell from a c statistic of 0.78 to 0.71 at an external hospital, where 58 percent boarded more than four hours against a mean predicted risk of 44 percent.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals; different model from the one in use here.

annotations.keyFindings: At the vendor threshold a commercial tool had sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.71 across three external hospitals; sensitivity was 0.49 at night and 0.66 by day.
annotations.limitations: Three hospitals; tool version may differ from the local one.

annotations.keyFindings: Mean boarding hours fell from 6.2 to 5.4 after a command centre opened, without assessment of flag accuracy.

Occupancy explained most variation in boarding; patient characteristics raised the c statistic only from 0.74 to 0.76; boarding over four hours occurred on 81 percent of days above 92 percent occupancy.
Sensitivity was 0.68 for medical and 0.51 for surgical admissions at a fixed threshold, and lowest between midnight and 06:00.
Departure timestamps ran on average 22 minutes late and were missing for 7 percent of admissions, misclassifying about 5 percent near the four-hour threshold.

claims.text: In an external validation at three hospitals, a commercial boarding tool at the vendor's threshold had sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.71, with sensitivity 0.49 for night-time admission decisions.
claims.passage: sensitivity for boarding of four hours or more was 0.62 (95 percent CI 0.60 to 0.64) and specificity 0.71
claims.interpretation: Planning values for the local evaluation; night performance must be reported separately.

synthesis: Six retrieved records from the second search, appraised at abstract level; the first search reported two hits but returned no records, and four model leads remain unchecked. External validation of a commercial boarding tool found moderate sensitivity and specificity at the vendor threshold, with much lower sensitivity at night; a developed model lost discrimination and calibration at an external hospital; sensitivity differed by admitting service; and occupancy, rather than patient characteristics, explained most boarding variation. Timestamps used as the reference standard are late and sometimes missing, which misclassifies patients near the four-hour threshold. A command centre was followed by fewer boarding hours in one hospital, but no study linked flag accuracy to that change. The records support a local accuracy study with a documented reference standard and results by time of day and service.
gradeRationale: Observational validation studies of different tools in other hospitals, with inconsistent calibration and indirectness to the local score; certainty that the local flag performs like the published tools is low.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; certainty low; four leads unverified.
